claim: The substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) sends axonal projections to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
source: Both the SNr and GPe are known to send axonal projections to the PPN (McElvain et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Roseberry et al., 2016; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2021; Dautan et al., 2021; Caggiano et al., 2018; Henrich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies that have demonstrated these anatomical projections.

claim: The globus pallidus externus (GPe) sends axonal projections to the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
source: Both the SNr and GPe are known to send axonal projections to the PPN (McElvain et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Roseberry et al., 2016; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2021; Dautan et al., 2021; Caggiano et al., 2018; Henrich et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies that have demonstrated these anatomical projections.

claim: SNr and GPe have monosynaptic connections to PPN cholinergic neurons.
source: Previous studies have identified SNr and GPe monosynaptic connections to the PPN cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons using rabies tracing (Zhao et al., 2022; Roseberry et al., 2016; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2021; Dautan et al., 2021; Caggiano et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple rabies tracing studies.

claim: SNr and GPe have monosynaptic connections to PPN glutamatergic neurons.
source: Previous studies have identified SNr and GPe monosynaptic connections to the PPN cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons using rabies tracing (Zhao et al., 2022; Roseberry et al., 2016; Huerta-Ocampo et al., 2021; Dautan et al., 2021; Caggiano et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple rabies tracing studies.

claim: SNr projections to MLR GABAergic neurons were identified but cannot be isolated to the PPN.
source: While SNr projections to MLR GABAergic neurons were identified but cannot be isolated to the PPN, GPe projections to the MLR GABAergic neurons were not detected (Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study that examined projections to the mesencephalic locomotor region.

claim: GPe projections to the MLR GABAergic neurons were not detected.
source: While SNr projections to MLR GABAergic neurons were identified but cannot be isolated to the PPN, GPe projections to the MLR GABAergic neurons were not detected (Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study that examined projections to the mesencephalic locomotor region.

claim: The PPN has three molecularly defined cell types, distinguished by their major neurotransmitter.
source: It has three molecularly defined cell types, distinguished by their major neurotransmitter (Wang and Morales, 2009) and distinct rostral and caudal topography.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing PPN cell types.

claim: Cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons are more densely packed in the caudal PPN.
source: While cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons are more densely packed in the caudal PPN, GABAergic neurons are more densely packed in the rostral PPN (Wang and Morales, 2009; Mena-Segovia et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing the anatomical distribution of PPN cell types.

claim: GABAergic neurons are more densely packed in the rostral PPN.
source: While cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons are more densely packed in the caudal PPN, GABAergic neurons are more densely packed in the rostral PPN (Wang and Morales, 2009; Mena-Segovia et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing the anatomical distribution of PPN cell types.

claim: Molecularly defined PPN populations display very minimal overlap.
source: These molecularly defined populations display very minimal overlap (Wang and Morales, 2009; Yoo et al., 2017; Steinkellner et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing the molecular identity of PPN neurons.

claim: The unique topography of the PPN has been conserved across species.
source: This unique topography has been conserved across species (Martinez-Gonzalez et al., 2011; Alam et al., 2011; Marín et al., 1998), but it is unknown how the basal ganglia connects to each of the distinct cell types in the rostral and caudal PPN regions to modulate locomotor and valence outputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: SNr axons appear in both the rostral and caudal PPN.
source: We found that SNr axons appear in both the rostral and caudal PPN.
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations from the study's imaging experiments.

claim: SNr axons fill the rostral PPN evenly but appear more distinctly clustered in specific areas of the caudal PPN.
source: The SNr axons fill the rostral PPN evenly but appear more distinctly clustered in specific areas of the caudal PPN (Figure 1B), whereas GPe axonal projections more densely fill the caudal region and strikingly avoid the rostral region (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations from confocal imaging shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GPe axonal projections more densely fill the caudal region and strikingly avoid the rostral region of the PPN.
source: The SNr axons fill the rostral PPN evenly but appear more distinctly clustered in specific areas of the caudal PPN (Figure 1B), whereas GPe axonal projections more densely fill the caudal region and strikingly avoid the rostral region (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical observations from confocal imaging shown in Figure 1D.

claim: All rostral cholinergic PPN neurons (19/19 cells) responded to SNr axon activation with an observable oIPSC.
source: We found that all rostral (n=19/19 cells, N=6 mice) and essentially all caudal (n=26/27, N=6) recorded cholinergic PPN neurons responded to SNr axon activation with an observable oIPSC (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and cholinergic PPN neurons.

claim: Essentially all caudal cholinergic PPN neurons (26/27 cells) responded to SNr axon activation with an observable oIPSC.
source: We found that all rostral (n=19/19 cells, N=6 mice) and essentially all caudal (n=26/27, N=6) recorded cholinergic PPN neurons responded to SNr axon activation with an observable oIPSC (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and cholinergic PPN neurons.

claim: There was no difference in amplitude of the first oIPSC in the stimulus train between rostral vs caudal cholinergic neurons.
source: There was no difference in amplitude of the first oIPSC in the stimulus train between rostral vs caudal cholinergic neurons (mean ± SEM; first oIPSC n=15 Rostral: 92.6±18 pA, n=20 Caudal: 115.2±17 pA; unpaired t-test, t=0.9041, df = 33, CI –28.4–73.7, p=0.3725; p=0.3725; Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal neurons.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of the peak of the first two currents in the stimulation train did not differ between rostral and caudal cholinergic neurons.
source: In addition, the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of the peak of the first two currents in the stimulation train did not differ (mean ± SEM; PPR n=15 Rostral: 0.96±0.04, n=20 Caudal: 0.97±0.05; unpaired t-test, t=0.1082, df = 33, CI –0.13–0.14, p=0.9145; Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing short-term synaptic plasticity.

claim: SNr synaptic inputs onto cholinergic neurons do not undergo significant short-term synaptic plasticity in either the rostral or caudal PPN.
source: SNr synaptic inputs onto cholinergic neurons do not undergo significant short-term synaptic plasticity in either the rostral or caudal PPN.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of normalized current amplitudes and paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: There was no significant difference between the percent frequency change in rostral and caudal cholinergic neurons during SNr axon stimulation.
source: However, there was no significant difference between the percent frequency change in rostral and caudal neurons during SNr axon stimulation (mean ± SEM; %Frequency n=14 Rostral: During Stimulation 35.62 ± 8.87%, Post Stimulation 136.1 ± 7.803%; n=23 Caudal: During Stimulation 52.11 ± 8.43%, Post Stimulation 119.1 ± 4.614%; two-way ANOVA, StimulationF(1, 35)=81.9 p<0.0001, RegionF(1, 35)=0.002052 p=0.9641, InteractionF(1, 35)=3.273 p=0.0790; Figure 2K)
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Rostral cholinergic neurons had greater rebound activity compared with caudal cholinergic neurons.
source: However, rostral cholinergic neurons had greater rebound activity compared with caudal cholinergic neurons as measured by the absolute change in rebound frequency [median (IQR); ΔRebFrq n=14 Rostral: 1.64 Hz (1.00–2.17 Hz), n=22 Caudal: 0.83 Hz (0.42–1.14 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=79, p=0.0142; Figure 2M].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of rebound firing frequency after inhibition.

claim: There is a weak but significant negative correlation between the frequency decrease during SNr axon stimulation and the rebound frequency increase in cholinergic PPN neurons.
source: We found a weak but significant negative correlation between the frequency decrease during SNr axon stimulation and the rebound frequency increase (Spearman r=−0.372, p=0.039, Figure 2N and O).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: All rostral GABAergic PPN neurons (12/12) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
source: We found that all rostral (n=12/12, N=6) and most caudal (n=20/22, N=6) recorded GABAergic PPN neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and GABAergic PPN neurons.

claim: Most caudal GABAergic PPN neurons (20/22) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
source: We found that all rostral (n=12/12, N=6) and most caudal (n=20/22, N=6) recorded GABAergic PPN neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and GABAergic PPN neurons.

claim: The first oIPSC showed no difference between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons receiving SNr input.
source: The oIPSC amplitudes across the 2 s stimulation as well as the first oIPSC showed no difference between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=9 Rostral: 76.5 pA (27.0–209.9 pA), n=13 Caudal: 59.7 pA (37.7–269.7 pA); Mann Whitney, U=50, p=0.6005; Figure 3C and D].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons.

claim: There were no significant differences in short-term synaptic plasticity between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons receiving SNr input.
source: We also did not observe significant differences in short-term synaptic plasticity between rostral and caudal GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); PPR n=9 Rostral: 1.01 (0.88–1.16), n=13 Caudal: 1.06 (0.96–1.15); Mann Whitney, U=48, p=0.5123; Figure 3F and G].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The percent inhibition of GABAergic PPN neurons was not significantly different between rostral and caudal neurons during SNr stimulation.
source: The percent inhibition was not significantly different between rostral and caudal neurons (mean ± SEM; %Frequency n=7 Rostral: During Stimulation 37.91 ± 15.91%, Post Stimulation 100.0 ± 14.57%; n=19 Caudal: During Stimulation 30.68 ± 8.03%, Post Stimulation 113.2 ± 5.187%; two-way ANOVA, StimulationF(1, 24)=44.63 p<0.0001, RegionF(1, 24)=0.09642 p=0.7588, InteractionF(1, 24)=0.8841 p=0.3565; Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between PPR and the pre-optical stimulation frequency in GABAergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found a significant negative correlation between PPR and the pre-optical stimulation frequency (Pre-Opto Frq, Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: All rostral glutamatergic PPN neurons (19/19) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
source: Similar to our findings in cholinergic and GABAergic neurons, we found that all rostral (n=19/19, N=6) and all caudal (n=28/28, N=6) recorded glutamatergic neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claim: All caudal glutamatergic PPN neurons (28/28) received inhibitory input from the SNr.
source: Similar to our findings in cholinergic and GABAergic neurons, we found that all rostral (n=19/19, N=6) and all caudal (n=28/28, N=6) recorded glutamatergic neurons received inhibitory input from the SNr (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing connectivity between SNr and glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claim: The median first oIPSC measured in caudal glutamatergic neurons was significantly larger than those recorded in rostral neurons.
source: The median first oIPSC measured in caudal glutamatergic neurons was also significantly larger than those recorded in rostral neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=13 Rostral: 61.6 pA (19.2–113.9 pA), n=13 Caudal: 313.5 pA (143.8–729.1 pA); Mann Whitney, U=29, p=0.0035; Figure 4D].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing rostral and caudal glutamatergic neurons.

claim: A 'hotspot' of strong SNr inhibition exists in a medial-caudal group of glutamatergic neurons.
source: After post-hoc staining for the cholinergic PPN and mapping the location of each recorded glutamatergic PPN neuron as described above, we identified a 'hotspot' of strong SNr inhibition in a medial-caudal group of glutamatergic neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on anatomical mapping of recorded neurons combined with electrophysiological data.

claim: The absolute frequency decrease was significantly larger in caudal glutamatergic neurons compared to rostral neurons during SNr stimulation.
source: we found that the absolute frequency decrease was significantly larger in caudal glutamatergic neurons compared to rostral neurons during SNr stimulation [median (IQR); ΔFrq During Opto n=13 Rostral: –3.21 Hz (−12.21 to –1.95 Hz), n=17 Caudal: –14.08 Hz (−20.04 to –6.07 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=55, p=0.0197; Figure 4J].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Caudal glutamatergic neurons fire faster than rostral glutamatergic neurons.
source: We found that caudal glutamatergic neurons fire faster than rostral glutamatergic neurons [median (IQR); Spontaneous Frequency n=11 Rostral: 6.8 Hz (5.4–17.2 Hz), n=16 Caudal: 20.6 Hz (11.2–37.2 Hz); Mann Whitney, U=45, p=0.0343; Figure 4K].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of spontaneous firing frequencies in glutamatergic PPN neurons.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the PPR and frequency change during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
source: Interestingly, there was a weak but significant positive correlation between the PPR and frequency change during stimulation, showing that input displaying short-term synaptic depression occurs in neurons with greater decreases in firing frequency (Spearman r=0.486, p=0.030; Figure 4M).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: SNr-mediated oIPSCs with larger amplitudes are correlated with greater decreases in firing frequency during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons.
source: As expected, SNr-mediated oIPSCs with larger amplitudes are correlated with greater decreases in firing frequency during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.841, p<0.00001; Figure 4N).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Greater pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with larger frequency decreases during stimulation in glutamatergic PPN neurons.
source: Greater pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with larger frequency decreases during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.791, p<0.0001; Figure 4O).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude in glutamatergic PPN neurons receiving SNr input.
source: Surprisingly, however, pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude (Spearman r=0.818, p<0.0001; Figure 4P), indicating that the SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
source: Surprisingly, however, pre-optical stimulation firing frequency is correlated with the first oIPSC amplitude (Spearman r=0.818, p<0.0001; Figure 4P), indicating that the SNr is more strongly connected to glutamatergic PPN neurons with faster firing rates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between firing frequency and synaptic strength.

claim: The median amplitude of the first SNr-mediated oIPSC was the same among rostral PPN neurons irrespective of cell type.
source: We found that the median amplitude of the first SNr-mediated oIPSC was the same among rostral PPN neurons irrespective of cell type [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=15 ChAT+: 74.7 pA (44.5–136.5 pA), n=9 Vgat+: 76.5 pA (27.0–209.9 pA), n=13 Vglut2+: 61.6 pA (19.2–113.9 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,34)=0.7002 p=0.7046; Figure 5A].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing SNr input strength across different cell types in the rostral PPN.

claim: The SNr-mediated oIPSCs in caudal glutamatergic neurons were significantly larger than in cholinergic and GABAergic caudal PPN neurons.
source: We found that the SNr-mediated oIPSCs in caudal glutamatergic neurons were significantly larger than in cholinergic and GABAergic caudal PPN neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=20 ChAT+: 109.3 pA (58.5–168.6 pA), n=12 Vgat+: 59.7 pA (37.7–269.7 pA), n=13 Vglut2+: 313.5 pA (143.8–729.1 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,43)=8.717 p=0.0128; Dunn's test, ChAT +vs Vgat +p = 0.6409, ChAT +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0042, Vgat +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0295; Figure 5C].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing SNr input strength across different cell types in the caudal PPN.

claim: The absolute frequency decrease during stimulation in caudal glutamatergic neurons was larger than both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons.
source: The absolute frequency decrease during stimulation in caudal glutamatergic neurons was larger than both cholinergic and GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); ΔFrq During Opto n=23 ChAT+: –2.10 Hz (−3.11 to –0.84 Hz), n=19 Vgat+: –4.29 Hz (−11.02 to –2.94 Hz), n=17 Vglut2+: –14.08 Hz (−20.04 to –6.07 Hz); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,56)=24.99 p<0.0001; Dunn's test, ChAT +vs Vgat +p = 0.0049, ChAT +vs Vglut2 +p < 0.0001, Vgat +vs Vglut2 +p = 0.0332; Figure 5D].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis comparing the impact of SNr stimulation on firing frequency across different cell types in the caudal PPN.

claim: Very few rostral PPN neurons received synaptic input from the GPe.
source: As predicted by the low density of GPe axons present in the rostral PPN (Figure 1D), very few rostral PPN neurons received synaptic input from the GPe.
evidence: The claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing low connectivity between GPe and rostral PPN neurons, consistent with anatomical observations.

claim: The GPe preferentially targets caudal PPN neurons compared to rostral neurons.
source: These findings show that the GPe preferentially targets caudal PPN neurons compared to rostral neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on connectivity data showing higher percentages of connected caudal neurons compared to rostral neurons.

claim: The percentage of connected caudal neurons was greater than the percentage of connected rostral neurons in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons receiving GPe input.
source: The percentage of connected caudal neurons was greater than the percentage of connected rostral neurons in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons (one-sided Fisher's exact test; Vgat: OR = 0.2857, CI = 0.09190–0.9391, p=0.047; Vglut2: OR = 0.1637, CI = 0.05069–0.5767, p=0.0033; Figure 6Cii and iii)
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of connectivity proportions between rostral and caudal regions.

claim: The GPe has essentially no direct effect on the cholinergic PPN neural population.
source: These findings indicate that the GPe has essentially no direct effect on the cholinergic PPN neural population.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that GPe-mediated currents in cholinergic neurons were small and had negligible effects on firing frequency.

claim: There was no significant difference in the first oIPSC measured in GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons receiving GPe input.
source: While there was no significant difference in the first oIPSC measured in GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons [median (IQR); first oIPSC n=19 Vgat+: 24.77 pA (6.72–54.17 pA), n=15 Vglut2+: 65.71 pA (14.50–133.4 pA); Kruskal-Wallis, H(2,37)=3.050, p=0.2176; Figure 6E]
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data comparing GPe input strength to different cell types.

claim: The GPe-mediated inhibitory input to glutamatergic neurons displayed a significantly lower PPR than to GABAergic neurons.
source: The GPe-mediated inhibitory input to glutamatergic neurons displayed a significantly lower PPR than to GABAergic neurons [median (IQR); PPR n=19 Vgat+: 0.97 (0.76–1.2), n=15 Vglut2+: 0.81 (0.55–0.93); Mann-Whitney, U=76, p=0.0206; Figure 6G].
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of paired-pulse ratios from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: There was no statistical difference between GPe inhibition of firing frequency in caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons.
source: We found no statistical difference between GPe inhibition of firing frequency in caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of firing frequency changes during GPe stimulation.

claim: Among GABAergic neurons receiving GPe inhibition, the amplitude of the first oIPSC is significantly correlated with the absolute change in frequency during stimulation.
source: Among GABAergic neurons receiving GPe inhibition, we found that the amplitude of the first oIPSC is significantly correlated with the absolute change in frequency during stimulation (Spearman r=−0.627, p=0.044, Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: GPe inhibition of the glutamatergic neurons showed a significant correlation between the absolute change in frequency during stimulation and pre-stimulation firing frequency.
source: GPe inhibition of the glutamatergic neurons showed a significant correlation between the absolute change in frequency during stimulation and pre-stimulation firing frequency (Spearman r=−0.648, p=0.014, Figure 6M).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled in the open field.
source: Specifically, stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled, while stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled [mean ± SEM; N=9 (3M, 6 F) Control (Ctrl): 2.22±0.24 m, N=8 (5M, 3 F) SNr: 4.11±0.51 m, N=9 (4M, 5 F) GPe: 0.57±0.18 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0263, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p=0.0002; Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Videos 1 and 2].
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled in the open field.
source: Specifically, stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN increased distance traveled, while stimulation of GPe axons in the PPN decreased distance traveled [mean ± SEM; N=9 (3M, 6 F) Control (Ctrl): 2.22±0.24 m, N=8 (5M, 3 F) SNr: 4.11±0.51 m, N=9 (4M, 5 F) GPe: 0.57±0.18 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0263, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p=0.0002; Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Videos 1 and 2].
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated in the RTPP task.
source: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated, but preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated (mean ± SEM; N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.0%, N=9 (5M, 4 F) SNr: 23.99 ± 5.2%, N=10 (5M, 5 F) GPe: 76.11 ± 3.7%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0437, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p<0.0001, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F, see Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from real-time place preference experiments.

claim: Mice preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated in the RTPP task.
source: Mice avoided the stimulated chamber when the SNr axons were stimulated, but preferred the stimulated chamber when the GPe axons were stimulated (mean ± SEM; N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.0%, N=9 (5M, 4 F) SNr: 23.99 ± 5.2%, N=10 (5M, 5 F) GPe: 76.11 ± 3.7%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr4.25mW p=0.0437, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe4.25mW p<0.0001, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F, see Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from real-time place preference experiments.

claim: The locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation.
source: We found that the locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation, but GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion (mean ± SEM; distance traveled N=9 (3M, 6 F) Ctrl: 2.22±0.24 m, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 2.24±0.50 m, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 1.09±0.22 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81; p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p>0.999, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0131; Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using low laser power to control for antidromic stimulation.

claim: GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion during low power stimulation.
source: We found that the locomotion effect of SNr stimulation over the PPN was no longer present during low power stimulation, but GPe stimulation still significantly decreased locomotion (mean ± SEM; distance traveled N=9 (3M, 6 F) Ctrl: 2.22±0.24 m, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 2.24±0.50 m, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 1.09±0.22 m; Welch ANOVAW(4.00, 15.86)=14.81; p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p>0.999, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0131; Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using low laser power to control for antidromic stimulation.

claim: SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level during low power stimulation in the RTPP task.
source: In the RTPP task, SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level and GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference (mean ± SEM; % time in stimulation zone N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.1%, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 27.72 ± 4.0%, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 68.41 ± 8.5%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using low laser power.

claim: GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference during low power stimulation in the RTPP task.
source: In the RTPP task, SNr axon stimulation continued to evoke place aversion at the trend level and GPe axon stimulation continued to significantly evoke place preference (mean ± SEM; % time in stimulation zone N=16 (6M, 10 F) Ctrl: 40.76 ± 2.1%, N=6 (3M, 3 F) SNr: 27.72 ± 4.0%, N=8 (4M, 4 F) GPe: 68.41 ± 8.5%; Welch ANOVAW(4.00,16.95)=26.73, p<0.0001; Dunnett's test, Ctrl4.25mW vs SNr0.25mW p=0.0695, Ctrl4.25mW vs GPe0.25mW p=0.0467; Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using low laser power.

claim: Decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN.
source: These findings show that decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN, while aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that effects persist at low laser power, suggesting local rather than antidromic effects.

claim: Aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
source: These findings show that decreased locomotion and place preference are mediated by GPe inhibition of the PPN, while aversion is mediated by SNr inhibition of the PPN.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that aversion persists at low laser power, suggesting local rather than antidromic effects.

claim: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power.
source: We found that selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and had no effect on locomotion at low power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claim: Selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN had no effect on locomotion at low power.
source: We found that selective stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN increased locomotion at high laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A) and had no effect on locomotion at low power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from open field experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claim: Stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN did not cause place aversion, but rather induced real-time place preference at both high and low laser power.
source: On the other hand, we found that stimulation of dopaminergic axons in the PPN did not cause place aversion, but rather induced real-time place preference at both high and low laser power (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data from RTPP experiments using DAT-cre mice to selectively stimulate dopaminergic neurons.

claim: The nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN.
source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dopaminergic stimulation increases locomotion at high but not low power, suggesting effects outside the PPN.

claim: Dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding.
source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place preference with dopaminergic stimulation.

claim: Total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
source: Together, these findings show that the nigral increase in locomotion is not mediated through the PPN, and that dopaminergic input from the SNc to the PPN is rewarding while total input from the substantia nigra to the PPN is aversive.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place aversion with non-selective nigral stimulation.

claim: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion.
source: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion and the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance it.
evidence: The claim refers to established models in the field of basal ganglia function.

claim: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance locomotion.
source: The canonical basal ganglia model predicts that the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) will inhibit locomotion and the globus pallidus externa (GPe) will enhance it.
evidence: The claim refers to established models in the field of basal ganglia function.

claim: The GPe exerts non-canonical effects on locomotion through inhibition of the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
source: In mice, we use in vivo optogenetics to show that the GPe exerts non-canonical effects on locomotion while the SNr has no gross motor impact through inhibition of the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing that GPe stimulation decreases rather than increases locomotion.

claim: The SNr has no gross motor impact through inhibition of the PPN.
source: In mice, we use in vivo optogenetics to show that the GPe exerts non-canonical effects on locomotion while the SNr has no gross motor impact through inhibition of the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN).
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing no locomotor effect at low laser power stimulation of SNr axons in the PPN.

claim: The SNr and GPe mediate opposing effects on reward.
source: We show that these structures mediate opposing effects on reward and that activation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopaminergic axons in the PPN is rewarding.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place aversion with SNr stimulation and place preference with GPe stimulation.

claim: Activation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopaminergic axons in the PPN is rewarding.
source: We show that these structures mediate opposing effects on reward and that activation of substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopaminergic axons in the PPN is rewarding.
evidence: The claim is based on behavioral data showing place preference with selective dopaminergic stimulation.

claim: The SNr inhibits all PPN subtypes but most strongly inhibits caudal glutamatergic neurons.
source: The SNr inhibits all PPN subtypes but most strongly inhibits caudal glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on comprehensive electrophysiological data comparing SNr input across different PPN cell types and regions.

claim: The GPe selectively inhibits caudal glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, avoiding both cholinergic and rostral cells.
source: The GPe selectively inhibits caudal glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons, avoiding both cholinergic and rostral cells.
evidence: The claim is based on comprehensive electrophysiological data showing selective connectivity patterns of GPe to PPN.

claim: The PPN has been implicated in locomotor control and valence processing.
source: The PPN has been implicated in locomotor control and valence processing (Ryczko, 2024; Bastos-Gonçalves et al., 2024; Mena-Segovia and Bolam, 2017; French and Muthusamy, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles and studies on PPN function.

claim: Optogenetic manipulations of the molecularly defined PPN cell types have resulted in variable, and sometimes contradictory, locomotor and valence behaviors.
source: Optogenetic manipulations of the molecularly defined PPN cell types have resulted in variable, and sometimes contradictory, locomotor and valence behaviors (Yoo et al., 2017; Roseberry et al., 2016; Dautan et al., 2021; Caggiano et al., 2018; Goñi-Erro et al., 2023; Masini and Kiehn, 2022; Gut et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024; Josset et al., 2018; Tello et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2016; Dautan et al., 2016; Ferreira-Pinto et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024; Hormigo et al., 2019; Hormigo et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies with varying results.

claim: Recent studies have refined understanding of opposing behavioral effects by selectively stimulating the rostral or caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons.
source: More recent studies have refined our understanding of these opposing behavioral effects by selectively stimulating the rostral or caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons (Goñi-Erro et al., 2023; Masini and Kiehn, 2022; Gut et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies examining regional differences in PPN function.

claim: Direct stimulation of molecularly defined SNr and GPe subpopulations can have distinct effects on locomotion and valence.
source: In the basal ganglia, direct stimulation of molecularly defined SNr and GPe subpopulations can also have distinct effects on locomotion and valence (Rizzi and Tan, 2019; Liu et al., 2023; Galaj et al., 2020; Mastro et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2018; Pamukcu et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2021; Aristieta et al., 2021; Isett et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the functional heterogeneity of basal ganglia neurons.

claim: Post-inhibitory rebound firing has been observed in the PPN as well as other brainstem structures.
source: Post-inhibitory rebound firing has been observed in the PPN as well as other brainstem structures (Baksa et al., 2019; Granata and Kitai, 1991; Kang and Kitai, 1990; Evans et al., 2017; Villalobos and Basso, 2022; Rajaram et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2022; Beaver and Evans, 2025)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting rebound firing in PPN and related structures.

claim: Rebound firing is associated with greater excitability, temporal encoding, and generation of oscillatory activity.
source: and is associated with greater excitability, temporal encoding, and generation of oscillatory activity (Sivaramakrishnan and Lynch, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the functional significance of rebound firing.

claim: Rostral cholinergic neurons tend to have stronger intrinsic rebound activity compared to caudal neurons.
source: This aligns with previous findings showing that rostral cholinergic neurons tend to have stronger intrinsic rebound activity compared to caudal neurons (Baksa et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study characterizing intrinsic properties of PPN neurons.

claim: Stimulating caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons increases locomotion.
source: Because stimulating the caudal GABAergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons increases locomotion (Masini and Kiehn, 2022), GPe selective inhibition of these caudal neurons could explain our behavioral experiments showing that stimulation of GPe axons over the PPN decreases locomotion.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the locomotor effects of stimulating specific PPN populations.

claim: Selectively stimulating the Npas1+ or FoxP2+ subpopulations in the GPe decreases locomotion.
source: Aligned with our findings, selectively stimulating the Npas1 +or FoxP2 +subpopulations in the GPe decreases locomotion (Pamukcu et al., 2020; Aristieta et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the functional heterogeneity of GPe neurons.

claim: Direct stimulation of the PV+ GPe neurons increases locomotion.
source: Some groups have found that direct stimulation of the PV +GPe neurons increases locomotion (Pamukcu et al., 2020; Lilascharoen et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the functional properties of PV+ GPe neurons.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ GPe neurons can increase locomotion.
source: however, one study shows that inhibition of PV +GPe neurons can increase locomotion (Isett et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study showing complex effects of PV+ GPe neuron manipulation.

claim: Direct somatic stimulation of PV+ and GAD2+ SNr neurons that send axon collaterals to the PPN decreases gross locomotor movement.
source: However, the SNr canonically suppresses movement and the direct somatic stimulation of PV +and GAD2 +SNr neurons that send axon collaterals to the PPN (McElvain et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020) decreases gross locomotor movement (Rizzi and Tan, 2019; Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the locomotor effects of SNr neuron stimulation.

claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons send axons to both the PPN and striatum.
source: This is consistent with previous literature showing that SNc dopaminergic neurons send axons to both the PPN and striatum (Ryczko et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the anatomical projections of SNc neurons.

claim: Direct stimulation of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons can increase movement initiation and vigor.
source: and that direct stimulation of nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons can increase movement initiation and vigor (da Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the functional effects of dopaminergic neuron stimulation.

claim: Inhibition of Vgat+ SNr neurons has been shown to increase place preference.
source: Inhibition of Vgat +SNr neurons has been shown to increase place preference (Galaj et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the valence effects of SNr neuron manipulation.

claim: Direct stimulation of Vgat+ SNr neurons has no effect on place preference.
source: while its direct stimulation has no effect (Rizzi and Tan, 2019; Galaj et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies examining the valence effects of SNr neuron stimulation.

claim: Selective stimulation of the PV+ SNr neurons induces aversion in RTPP.
source: However, selective stimulation of the PV +SNr neurons induces aversion in RTPP (Rizzi and Tan, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the valence effects of PV+ SNr neuron stimulation.

claim: Inhibition of PV+ GPe neurons induced aversion in RTPP.
source: One recent study shows that inhibition of PV +GPe neurons induced aversion while inhibition of Npas1 +GPe neurons induced place preference in RTPP (Isett et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the valence effects of GPe neuron manipulation.

claim: Inhibition of Npas1+ GPe neurons induced place preference in RTPP.
source: One recent study shows that inhibition of PV +GPe neurons induced aversion while inhibition of Npas1 +GPe neurons induced place preference in RTPP (Isett et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the valence effects of GPe neuron manipulation.

claim: The cholinergic PPN neurons are implicated in positive valence with place preference and increased lever pressing through their projections to the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: The cholinergic PPN neurons are implicated in positive valence with place preference and increased lever pressing through their projections to the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Xiao et al., 2016; Dautan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on the role of cholinergic PPN neurons in reward processing.

claim: Direct inhibition of the cholinergic PPN neurons evokes place aversion.
source: Aligned with our findings, direct inhibition of the cholinergic PPN neurons evokes place aversion (Xiao et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the valence effects of inhibiting cholinergic PPN neurons.

claim: Direct stimulation of the glutamatergic PPN neurons has been implicated in positive valence with increased reinforcement behavior.
source: Direct stimulation of the glutamatergic PPN neurons has also been implicated in positive valence with increased reinforcement behavior (Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on the role of glutamatergic PPN neurons in reward processing.

claim: Both the cholinergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons directly influence dopamine release in the striatum and dopaminergic neuron activity in the SNc and VTA.
source: Both the cholinergic and glutamatergic PPN neurons directly influence dopamine release in the striatum and dopaminergic neuron activity in the SNc and VTA (Yoo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2016; Dautan et al., 2016; Forster and Blaha, 2003; Estakhr et al., 2017; Galtieri et al., 2017; Futami et al., 1995; Good and Lupica, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on the functional connections between PPN and dopaminergic systems.

claim: The caudal PPN neurons are thought to innervate the medial part of the SNc and the VTA.
source: Specifically, the caudal PPN neurons are thought to innervate the medial part of the SNc and the VTA (Martinez-Gonzalez et al., 2011; Good and Lupica, 2009), two major reward pathway hubs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies on PPN projections to dopaminergic regions.

claim: PPN neurons that excite amygdala nuclei evoke place avoidance.
source: For example, PPN neurons that excite amygdala nuclei evoke place avoidance (Liu et al., 2023; Aitta-aho et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on PPN projections to the amygdala and their behavioral effects.
